changes.summary: This is the Discord for the KC7 Foundation's free cyber-detective game, where players investigate simulated intrusions using realistic threat-actor data in Azure Data Explorer/Kusto. It's built to help students and career-changers with no background break into cybersecurity analysis and threat intelligence through hands-on scenarios, workshops, and peer support, and is very welcoming to complete beginners.
changes.reason: Added missing mentorship tag (activities list it); rewrote summary because it started with the server name.

changes.summary: A community-run server aimed at people getting into ethical hacking and IT/security broadly, covering CTF challenges, networking, cryptography, mobile security, and career discussion. It's explicitly pitched at newcomers with guidance on breaking into the field and runs its own CTF challenges with prizes.
changes.reason: Summary mentions mobile security but the tag was missing; also rewrote summary to stop it starting with the server name.

changes.summary: A volunteer-run 501(c)(3) nonprofit that hosts hands-on cybersecurity workshops, CTF nights, mentorship, and social events aimed at making the field approachable rather than intimidating. It welcomes all skill levels, from complete beginners and job-seekers to professionals who mentor, with free membership and both online and in-person activity.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: A hands-on cybersecurity learning community where members work through practical security challenges, CTFs, and mentoring together rather than just reading theory. It's pitched at people who learn by doing, from beginners picking up fundamentals to those looking for peer collaboration on harder challenges.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: A long-running Spanish-language community (since 2007) dedicated to information security and ethical hacking, predating Discord itself as a forum before moving there. It's a general hangout for Spanish-speaking hackers to discuss techniques and share knowledge, fitting those who want an established, veteran-run community rather than a structured beginner course.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: A community-run server for hackers and infosec enthusiasts of all skill levels, with a competitive CTF team registered on CTFtime. Beyond general chat, members get help with mock interviews, resume reviews, and breaking into a cybersecurity career, alongside live sessions and networking. It's aimed squarely at people trying to learn fundamentals and land their first infosec job.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: A small community-run server focused on raising awareness of scams and malware and helping members avoid them. People share warnings about active scams, discuss suspicious links and messages, and chat generally about staying safe online. It suits casual users wanting a lighter, scam-awareness-focused space rather than deep technical security training.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: An education-focused ethical hacking community, popular in Indonesia, that runs daily voice sessions plus weekly and monthly cybersecurity events. Members discuss general infosec topics, share bug bounty proof-of-concepts, and support each other's learning in a busy, active chat.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: A general cybersecurity chat and education community aimed at making security culture and learning accessible to beginners as well as more experienced enthusiasts. Members discuss security news, share resources, and can attend occasional webinars or workshops, making it suited to people wanting a casual entry point into infosec discussion rather than a structured program.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: Run by Mike, a security researcher and blogger, this community grew out of a CTF-focused meet-up group and now covers infosec, technology, and life topics on his blog and podcast. On Discord, members discuss security news and articles, share writeups, and talk shop with other practitioners. It suits people already working in or studying infosec who want ongoing discussion rather than structured lessons.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: This is the official community Discord for TrustedSec, a well-known offensive security consultancy founded by David Kennedy, promoted through their podcast and social channels. Members chat with each other and sometimes TrustedSec staff about red teaming, pentesting, and security news. It suits working security professionals and students who want a large, active general-infosec crowd rather than structured beginner content.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: This is the main Discord hub for CryptoHack, a free, community-run platform for learning modern applied cryptography through hands-on programming challenges, covering those challenges, cryptography news, and general math/programming questions. New members answer a short cryptography-themed verification question to get in and can link their CryptoHack profile for special roles. It works well for people starting from zero on crypto as well as CTF players sharpening cryptography skills.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: This community grew out of a CTF team started in 2019 around The Blind Hacker's journey as a visually impaired infosec professional, and has become a broad mentoring community covering red team, blue team, sysadmin, and certifications. It welcomes people from complete beginners to working professionals and has dedicated channels for certs, jobs, and both offensive and defensive topics, making it a solid pick for beginners wanting a supportive, mentorship-oriented space.
changes.reason: Summary started with the server name.

changes.summary: This is the community hub for Pwned Labs, a Dubai-based cloud and AI security training platform offering hands-on labs, bootcamps with vendor-style certifications (AWS, Azure, GCP), and cyber ranges, where practitioners discuss cloud and AI attack and defense techniques and support each other's learning. It suits people specifically wanting to learn cloud security, from newcomers using the free academy tier up to advanced practitioners pursuing paid certifications. Some content and certifications require payment.

changes.summary: A broad, community-run cybersecurity server covering both offensive and defensive topics: CTFs, red team, blue team, web security, OSINT, reverse engineering, and bug bounty, alongside general programming and AI discussion. notes: general-learning: Additional items noticed but left unchanged: (1) hacktrace-ranges-and-training promotes an external 'ranges' product whose website returned an error and has no independent coverage — legitimacy is genuinely uncertain but it wasn't hidden since it still has real chat/challenge activity; worth a second look if you want a stricter bar. (2) republic-of-hackers has a documented 2024 incident where the server was compromised for a fake airdrop scam — kept listed (red_flags field already surfaces this) but flag to reviewers as a trust concern rather than a beginner-friendliness issue. (3) Beyond the two bf changes made (reverse-engineering, 0x00sec-official), several other servers with audience=[intermediate, advanced] and no beginner content are still scored bf=3 (malwaretech, sans-offensive-operations, shellsharks, trustedsec, cyber-security-centre) — by a strict reading of the bf-2 definition ('mostly intermediate/advanced') these arguably belong at 2, but I left them since their communities do field general questions in practice; consider a rubric decision on whether 'audience has no beginner' alone should force bf<=2. (4) arcadia's tie to bettercap is explicitly flagged in the data as unverified/mismatched with the official bettercap Discord invite — left as category general per the data's own uncertainty rather than recategorizing to 'tool'. (5) A handful of personal-creator-run servers (0xswezy, malwaretech, shellsharks) are categorized 'general' despite being built around one individual's brand; the 'creator' category exists in the taxonomy but is unused anywhere in this file, so I left these as-is for consistency with how similar entries were already categorized rather than guessing at an unused convention. (6) pen-ace-hacking-time and cybersecurity-artists are extremely small (81 and 202 members) with no independent verification, but neither meets an explicit exclusion criterion, so both were left listed with their existing red_flags notes.

ctf-appsec-redteam: Reviewed all 46 entries. Most bf/category/tag/region assignments are internally consistent and consistent with peer entries (e.g. the bug-bounty-platform cluster — bugcrowd, hackerone, intigriti, portswigger — all bf 3-4 with mixed audiences; the exploit-dev/redteam cluster — corelan, zero-point-security, 0x0539-net, redteam-alliance, covert-access-team — all bf 2 with intermediate/advanced audiences). No duplicates found. No entries met the hide criteria (all are genuinely security-relevant, no scams/NSFW/off-topic content), though 'code4rena' carries a red_flag about its listed invite having unusually low membership (34/2) relative to the platform's real size — left as-is since the researcher already flagged it and it's a data-quality caveat rather than a reason to exclude a legitimate platform. 'hack-different' (Apple jailbreak/reverse-engineering) doesn't cleanly fit any category — 'appsec' is a stretch since it's OS/hardware reverse engineering rather than application security — but no better category exists in the allowed list, so left unchanged. Did not verify actual spoken language of tcp1p-server since no web lookups were used; fixed the summary/language contradiction conservatively by editing the summary rather than guessing the language code.

creator-careers-affinity: No entries needed hiding (nothing off-topic, scammy, or unsafe) and no in-group duplicates found. Beginner-friendliness scores looked internally consistent given each server's stated activities/audience, so I left bf values alone even where borderline (e.g. security-weekly bf4, arcanum-discord bf4 despite paid-tier gating, critical-thinking-podcast bf3) rather than force changes without clear peer-outlier evidence. hack4u's region is 'global' despite being Spanish-language/Spain-associated content — left as-is since it plausibly serves the global Spanish-speaking diaspora rather than one country. overflow's red_flag already flags unverified official status, which seems appropriately cautious. All tag lists were within the 3-8 range and used only allowed tags, so no tag edits were needed beyond the category changes above.

tool-hardware-adjacent: No duplicates found. Borderline-relevance entries already self-flagged and left as-is: Open Source Hardware Association (red_flags notes limited security relevance), MSPs Я Us and CyberDrain (MSP/IT-admin focused, only adjacent to security -- kept since they touch security compliance/tooling). Offensive Appliances and Netgotchi are low-confidence listings (no public info found) but nothing indicates they're illegitimate or unsafe, so left un-hidden rather than guessing. Amass's activities list includes "hardware-help" which looks like a copy-paste artifact for a pure recon/software tool, but activities weren't in scope for this pass. Considered but did not change: Flipper-Devices/Kali-Linux-and-Friends bf=3 despite huge official scale (defensible given "tone varies by channel" caveat in their own summaries); Cardputer bf=3 despite "beginner questions somewhat off-topic" phrasing (has explicit beginner audience, unlike the downgraded OSCR).

blueteam-osint: Group is generally well-curated and consistent. A few things noticed but left unchanged:

- Many summaries open with the server's own name (CyberDefenders, LetsDefend, OSINT-FR, VX Feed, GlobalNews.Watch, Project Owl, SOC Prime, CORE.CTI, BosINT/OSINTNova). This is a widespread house-style pattern across roughly half the file rather than an isolated error, so rewriting all of them would exceed conservative-edit guidance; flagging the pattern instead of touching every instance. Only fixed the two cases (kase, cti-cyber-threat-intelligence) that also had a factual problem.
- bf ratings for the threat-intel/DFIR cluster (core-cti, cti-cyber-threat-intelligence, vx-feed at bf2 vs. threat-hunter-community, blue-team-labs-online, digital-forensics, forensic-focus, soc-prime at bf3) initially looked inconsistent since several use near-identical "not for absolute beginners" phrasing. On closer look the bf2 group are pure news/chat firehoses with no study-groups/workshops/challenges, while the bf3 group all have at least one structured learning activity (study-groups, workshops, or challenges) — this split is defensible and was left alone.
- 'careers' tag is inconsistently applied: digital-forensics and forensic-focus carry it (job-board activity), but letsdefend, centri, and cyberdefenders also have job-board activity without the tag. Didn't add it broadly since omission isn't clearly wrong, just an optional descriptor — worth a pass in a future consistency sweep.
- osint-fr carries a "students" tag that isn't strongly supported by its summary (researchers/journalists/professionals/hobbyists, not specifically students); left as a borderline call rather than a clear error.
- server-3 (Russian-language) is labeled region "europe" — geographically defensible for a Russian-speaking audience given no "asia" region option is used elsewhere in the schema, so left as is.
- faytuks-news-osint and globalnews-watch are general world-news/OSINT feeds with limited traditional infosec content; both already carry an appropriate red_flag/summary caveat and fit the osint category as defined, so not recommended for hiding.

conference-village-regional: Reviewed all ~130 entries in conference-village-regional.json. Overall quality is high and internally consistent for most fields (bf ratings mostly track audience/tags well: e.g. hexacon=1/advanced-only, comfycon-au/seckc/dc225/dc256=5 with explicit welcoming language, red-team-village/adversary-village=2-3 with intermediate+ audience). Main findings above concern (a) category inconsistency between near-identical single-conference BSides Discords -- some labeled 'conference', some 'regional' -- normalized to 'conference'; (b) DEF CON Group entries are consistently 'regional' except DC² which was mislabeled 'conference'; (c) two general hackerspaces (nyc-resistor, thelab-ms) whose own summaries say they are not security-specific, moved to 'adjacent'; (d) one bf outlier (northsec) brought in line with peer advanced-only conferences; (e) one missing tag (ru-security-club/mentorship); (f) two hide recommendations -- bsides-vilnius (invite goes to an unrelated conference, Elbsides Hamburg) and call-center-village (7-member effectively-dead invite).

Not changed, but noted for awareness:
- A large fraction of summaries across this whole file open with the server's own name (e.g. 'BSidesSLC is...', 'Hexacon is...', 'DC612 is...'). This is a pervasive stylistic pattern across nearly the entire batch rather than an isolated outlier, so rewriting all of them would far exceed a conservative change budget; left as-is except where combined with another issue.
- noisebridge and hacdc are borderline cases similar to nyc-resistor/thelab-ms (general hackerspaces where security is 'one of many topics'), but both still carry a general-infosec tag and more explicit security programming, so they were left as 'regional'.
- Region granularity is inconsistent (bsides-pakistan = 'asia' vs def-con-delhi-group = 'india') but not clearly wrong either way, so left alone.
- hackfest-ca's tags could arguably include lockpicking-physical/social-engineering given its named villages, but left as-is to stay conservative.
